claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a ferromagnetic fcc matrix and hexagonal C14 Laves precipitates.
The C14 Laves phase in FeCoNiTi is Ti-rich.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity below or capped near 100 Oe because their orbital moments are insufficient.
Coexistence with the C14 phase alters the magnetic ground state of the fcc FeCoNiTi phase through interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling.
The proposed interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling occurs between Fe, Co, and Ni sublattices and the Ti-rich C14 phase.
Ti in the C14 phase has a magnetic moment or antiferromagnetic ordering tendency different from that of the ferromagnetic fcc matrix.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling suppresses saturation magnetization by reducing the effective moment per atom or producing non-collinear interfacial spins.
The C14 phase is a hard intermetallic with high magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
C14 precipitates provide strong pinning sites for magnetic domain walls in FeCoNiTi.
Rapid quenching produces a high density of fcc/C14 interfaces and therefore a high density of magnetic pinning centers.
Multiphase decomposition or second-phase formation can coincide with increased coercivity and reduced saturation magnetization in a high-entropy alloy.
Multiphase alloys containing antiferromagnetic or hard-magnetic second phases generally have greater coercivity than corresponding single-phase alloys.
Reduced saturation magnetization lowers the demagnetizing field and thereby contributes to increased coercivity.
The combined effects of antiferromagnetic coupling and C14-mediated domain-wall pinning produce a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
The dual-phase alloy will have lower saturation magnetization than a single-phase fcc comparator at 400 K.
The proposed coercivity enhancement may disappear if the C14 phase is absent or its phase fraction is too low to supply sufficient pinning sites.
The magnetic effect should diminish as temperature approaches the Curie temperature of the fcc phase or the ordering temperature of the C14 phase.
Spin-resolved density-of-states calculations at the Fermi level for the fcc phase can test its proposed electronic and magnetic state.
A comparison among dual-phase, single-phase fcc, and C14-dominant alloys can isolate phase-specific magnetic behavior and transitions.
Observing coercivity below 150 Oe with no significant saturation-magnetization reduction in the dual-phase sample would falsify the proposed strong coupling and pinning mechanism.
